newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EIA sees 1 pct world annual oil price rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EIA sees 1 pct world annual oil price rise.

text.p: World oil prices should rise by one percent a year from 1995 levels through 2015, to $21 per barrel in constant 1995 dollars, adjusted for inflation, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said.
World oil demand should rise 2.1 percent annually from 69.4 million barrels per day in 1995 to 104.6 million bpd in 2015, the EIA said, which is an upward revision of about 5.7 million bpd for 2015.
Despite the stronger demand, new oil production possibilities should keep a lid on prices, the EIA said in its international outlook on 1995-2015.

The EIA lowered its oil price projection for 2015 by $5 per barrel from last year's projection, saying that even though recent prices were higher than projections for 2015, they "are not a harbinger of return to high and persistently rising oil price trajectory."
Oil's share of total energy consumption drops slightly in this forecast from 39 percent in 1995 to 38 percent in 2015, with slower projected growth in industrialized countries.

Industrialized countries' demand for oil should rise 1.1 percent annually in 1995-2015, reaching 52.3 million bpd, while developing countries' demand should rise by 3.5 percent annually and reach 42.7 million bpd.
Demand in the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe should rise by 2.6 percent annually, reaching 9.6 million bpd.
Production capacity of all members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) should climb from 36.2 million bpd in 2000 to 57.6 million bpd in 2015.
Non-OPEC production capacity should grow at a slower rate, from 45.2 million bpd in 2000 to 49.3 million bpd in 2015.

By 2015, the EIA said OPEC exports to industrialized countries should be 13.8 million bpd, up 8 million bpd from 1995, with more than three-fourths of that increase expected to come from the Gulf region.
OPEC exports to developing countries in that time should rise by more than 16 million bpd, with China alone accounting for more than 5 million bpd from OPEC by 2015.
